docs.why: trust boundaries are owned by State 0

phases.purpose: Establish what the application is before any code structure: goal, actors, primary actions, inputs, observable outputs, persistent data, external systems, constraints and open questions. No contracts, module paths or algorithms.
questions: Are goal, actors, primary actions, inputs, observable outputs, persistent data, external systems, constraints and open questions all stated?
Does every product promise name a concrete user action, its observable output and its failure outcome?
Is every unknown written as an open question rather than hidden behind an abstraction or an extension point?

docs.why: identity closure is required before State 2
model kinds, identity and the closed form a model takes in the specification

phases.purpose: Design the concepts and data shapes the application needs: start from domain meaning, then fields and types; every model has a reason, an owner and a source for each required field.
questions: For each model: why does it exist, who creates, reads and modifies it, and where does every required field come from?
Is every field needed by a stated requirement, and are concepts that change for different reasons kept as separate models?
Is any dict, Any, metadata bag or shared status field standing in for a structure not yet decided?
Is every interface, optional field and format branch required by a present product need rather than a future one?

docs.why: security review must close before State 3
a decided value needs one of three paths to generated code, or it stays a design fact outside the spec

phases.purpose: Separate what must always hold from what merely configures behaviour, and record each as an accepted decision. A decided value that code must read gets one of the three paths of SPEC_STANDARD 15.3.1; any other fact stays a design decision outside the spec.
questions: Which statements must always hold, and which values merely configure behaviour; is each recorded as an accepted decision?
Does each invariant name one future owning responsibility, and is every lifecycle-relevant state transition written explicitly?
Is every policy a declared rule, value, ordering or recorded open question rather than prose like 'best' or 'reasonable'?
For each decided value: which path of SPEC_STANDARD 15.3.1 carries it to code, or does it stay a design fact outside the spec?
Does every normative State 2 document hold at least one indexed accepted decision, so that the lint can see it?

docs.why: expand -> narrow -> references loop before assigning an owner
an exported function must not be named like a contract parameter, a model field or an everyday word: the projector infers imports by whole word

phases.purpose: Derive modules from ownership of complexity, rules and knowledge - never from screens, endpoints or verbs. A module is a small public surface over one hidden mechanism.
questions: Is each module justified by the knowledge and rules it owns rather than by a screen, endpoint, entity or verb?
Do its public capabilities rest on one hidden mechanism with one reason to change, or do they only share an entity name?
Does it hold several state machines, transaction topologies, disjoint dependency sets or consumer subsets that make it several modules?
Does any module own policy outside its role, merely forward arguments, or collect behaviour nobody else owns?
Is the public surface smaller than the hidden behaviour, and would any split trigger fire if this module were one file?

docs.why: only a Trace inputs section creates trace edges

phases.purpose: Tie every State 3 ownership claim to the State 2 decision it enforces, from normative text that was read, not from shared words.
questions: Is every ownership or relation claim backed by a normative source you read, not by a shared name or a mention hit?

docs.why: flow plan artifact and review gate

phases.purpose: Walk the few important end-to-end flows before fixing any API: who triggers, what crosses each boundary, who decides next, who produces each promised result and each failure.
questions: At each flow transition, are the crossing model, the next decision owner, the error translator and the cleanup duty named?
Does every major flow end in an observable result or an explicit failure produced by a named module, with no logic hidden in endpoints?
For every promised state, artifact or result in this flow, which single component produces it?

docs.why: internal is the export surface of a provider; module_internal is the minimal import surface of a consumer
every public operation has exactly one owning module

phases.purpose: Define only the operations other modules may call: owner, callers, the need it serves, and an output concrete enough to forbid an empty result.
questions: Does each public operation serve a real cross-module need, hide internal sequencing, and return an output concrete enough to forbid empty results?

docs.why: structured data closure feeds State 6 signatures
the ordered placement procedure; the first matching check wins
every leaf must be reachable; a reference names the smallest node
enum in models, data-provider constant, or runtime setting - and when an = address is legal
one home per leaf; array position is not an identifier; no computed values
the closed form of the data provider: value types, one exact entry - one scalar constant
the only path from a config leaf to generated code

phases.purpose: Place every accepted value in its one home before contracts are written (SPEC_STANDARD 15.2-15.4): an enum in models, a data-provider constant, or a runtime setting. A value with no path to code does not enter the specification.

docs.why: exact contract format
external facts require content-addressed evidence
a parameter named like another module's exported function becomes an import and shadows it
every name in type position resolves to exactly one origin

phases.purpose: Write exact typed signatures. If a contract needs a model that does not exist, return to State 1; do not keep uncertainty in dict, Any, object or speculative optional parameters.
questions: Does every argument have a clear source, every return value a consumer, and every function exactly one owning module?
Does any signature keep uncertainty through dict, Any, object, or optional parameters added only for hypothetical reuse?
Is any exported function named like a contract parameter, a model field or an everyday word that notes use as a word (SPEC_STANDARD 7)?

docs.why: post-contract persistence backend_ir handoff
router closure binds to canonical State 6 handlers
router context closure
final router IR is a deterministic projection

phases.conditional: implementation_obligations declares disposition local for a port interface

docs.why: emitter binding of deterministic backends
deterministic BLOCK checks and note grammar
propagating notes across split 80_notes*.md files
note form, the closed class registry, no inline data, no expressions
how a note names a value: = models.Enum, the imported X constant, or a settings field; = rules.x on product data stops the prompt build
a whole word equal to another module's export becomes a required import of this module
the generator receives a symbol and a type, never a value

phases.purpose: Write notes only after contracts and ownership are stable. A note states behaviour the signature does not: a placeholder implementation must contradict it. Notes name values by symbol, never repeat them.
questions: Could this function be implemented as return None, an empty value, a constant or plain forwarding without contradicting its notes?
Are its observable outcome, output field sources, failure behaviour, side effects and forbidden shortcuts all stated?
Does each MUST note name a specific condition, outcome, assignment or boundary that a stub implementation would violate?

docs.why: its module docstring states what a decision witness is and how coverage is counted
aggregate readiness gate and per-owner checks
the standard's own list of what a complete specification holds

phases.purpose: Materialise global_spec.json from the closed handoffs. Nothing is decided here: a product decision met during assembly goes back to the state that owns it.

docs.why: module review packet
adversarial semantic review handoff

phases.purpose: Review every assembled module slice. A structural zero-block result is not a semantic verdict: record the classification against the exact slice hash.

docs.why: read-only admission gate and export

phases.purpose: Operational, not a semantic state: prove against the exact target Factory checkout that the Factory will accept, cut and carry this specification, before anything is written there.

read_policy.rule: Read only the docs returned by `authoring next` for the current phase; the sequence, not a global reading list, owns which methodology text applies.
read_policy.questions: `questions` are the judgement a gate cannot make. Answer each in the state document before the gate; at most five per phase - a sixth means a gate is missing.
